question: What makes a disease 'non-communicable'?

options.A: It cannot be spread from person to person
options.B: It develops and resolves within a few days
options.C: It is caused strictly by bacterial infections
options.D: It only affects elderly people in urban areas

explanation: You got this! Non-communicable diseases are chronic conditions that don't pass from one person to another through contact or germs, unlike infections like malaria or typhoid. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T1#GNS313_U3_T1_h1)

question: In Nigeria, what do we mean by the 'double burden of disease'?

options.A: Having two different types of cancer simultaneously in one organ
options.B: Paying double taxes for healthcare services in public and private hospitals
options.C: Dealing with both infectious diseases and non-communicable diseases at the same time
options.D: Experiencing high rates of both malaria and severe malnutrition

explanation: Spot on! The double burden means our communities are fighting traditional infectious diseases (like malaria) while also seeing a sharp rise in chronic illnesses (like hypertension and diabetes). [learn more](GNS313_U3_T1#GNS313_U3_T1_h1)

question: Which of these is considered a metabolic risk factor for non-communicable diseases?
explanation: Great job! Metabolic risk factors happen inside the body's chemistry and biology, such as high blood pressure, high blood sugar, or extra body weight. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T1#GNS313_U3_T1_h2)

question: Why do social factors like poverty play such a big role in NCDs?

options.A: They ensure that patients always adhere strictly to their medication regimen
options.B: They directly cause genetic mutations that trigger cancer within weeks
options.C: They limit access to healthy foods, safe exercise spaces, and proper healthcare
options.D: They completely eliminate the risk of developing infectious diseases

explanation: Exactly! When money is tight, it becomes much harder to afford nutritious food, find safe places to exercise, or visit the clinic early for check-ups. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T1#GNS313_U3_T1_h2)

question: What is the main goal of primary prevention?

options.A: To rehabilitate a patient who suffered a stroke or paralysis
options.B: To cure a chronic illness that has lasted for many years
options.C: To prevent a disease from ever occurring in a healthy person
options.D: To screen a community for early signs of high blood sugar

explanation: You nailed it! Primary prevention is all about stopping health problems before they even start by promoting healthy habits and tackling risk factors. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T1#GNS313_U3_T1_h3)

question: You're a community nurse at a local market. Which activity is a great example of primary prevention for hypertension?

options.A: Admitting every market trader with high blood pressure to the intensive care unit
options.B: Distributing free blood pressure medication to people who already have severe stroke symptoms
options.C: Teaching market traders how to reduce salt in local meals and encouraging daily walks
options.D: Referencing advanced surgical guidelines for treating blocked coronary arteries

explanation: Brilliant! Teaching healthy eating and active living helps people protect their hearts before high blood pressure has a chance to develop. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T1#GNS313_U3_T1_h3)

question: What is the main objective of secondary prevention?

options.A: Early detection and prompt treatment of a disease to stop its progress
options.B: Providing end-of-life comfort care for terminally ill cancer patients
options.C: Promoting nationwide policies against tobacco farming and importation
options.D: Eliminating all genetic mutations that run in family lineages

explanation: Spot on! Secondary prevention is about catching a disease early through screenings so we can treat it quickly before complications arise. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T1#GNS313_U3_T1_h4)

question: Why is having a clear referral pathway so important during community health screenings?

options.A: To ensure individuals who screen positive actually receive further diagnosis and care
options.B: To prevent healthy people from attending community health outreaches
options.C: To reduce the total number of nurses required to work in primary care
options.D: To increase the financial cost of running the screening camp for organizers

explanation: You got it! Finding a high blood pressure reading at a screening is only the first step—we must guide the patient safely to a clinic for proper confirmation and care. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T1#GNS313_U3_T1_h4)

question: What is the main focus when managing non-communicable diseases in clinical practice?

options.A: Isolating the patient in a specialized ward to prevent spreading
options.B: Achieving a complete cure within a fourteen-day treatment window
options.C: Administering a short course of antibiotics to kill the pathogen
options.D: Long-term symptom control and prevention of complications

explanation: Correct! Because chronic conditions last a lifetime, our care focuses on keeping symptoms under control, protecting organs, and helping patients live well. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T1#GNS313_U3_T1_h5)

question: Why do many patients managing chronic NCDs also need psychological support?

options.A: Psychological therapy replaces the need for any blood pressure or diabetic drugs
options.B: Mental health counseling can completely reverse physical organ damage in diabetes
options.C: Depression is the physical pathogen that directly causes high blood pressure
options.D: Living with a lifelong, restricting illness frequently triggers depression and anxiety

explanation: That's right! Coping with a permanent illness, strict diets, and daily medication costs can be emotionally heavy, making mental health support just as important as physical care. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T1#GNS313_U3_T1_h5)

question: What is one of the biggest duties of a community health nurse when dealing with NCDs?

options.A: Manufacturing affordable insulin and blood pressure drugs in local clinics
options.B: Performing major neurosurgeries in rural primary health centers
options.C: Bridging the gap between formal health facilities and grassroots populations
options.D: Enforcing strict national prison sentences for people who eat junk food

explanation: Spot on! Community nurses take health education, screenings, and support right to the doorsteps and neighborhoods where people live. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T1#GNS313_U3_T1_h6)

question: A hypertensive patient keeps missing clinic days and stopped taking their drugs. As their nurse, what is your best next step?

options.A: Assume the patient is completely cured and stop calling their phone number
options.B: Conduct a home visit to discuss barriers to compliance and provide tailored education
options.C: Discharge the patient permanently from the clinic registry without further discussion
options.D: Report the patient to local law enforcement authorities for policy violation

explanation: Wonderful nursing judgment! Visiting them helps you find out why they stopped—maybe money is tight or side effects are bothering them—so you can help find a solution together. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T1#GNS313_U3_T1_h6)

question: Why do we need 'multisectoral collaboration' to effectively control NCDs?

options.A: Hospitals do not have enough medical equipment to treat infectious diseases
options.B: Government policies can only be implemented by doctors and surgeons
options.C: Nurses are not qualified to talk to patients about diet and exercise
options.D: Risk factors like poor diet, tobacco use, and physical inactivity require action from many societal sectors

explanation: You nailed it! Fighting NCDs goes beyond the hospital; it involves agriculture, education, finance, and urban planning working together as a team. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T1#GNS313_U3_T1_h7)

question: What is the main reason governments place heavy taxes on tobacco and sugary drinks?

options.A: To completely ban all agricultural farming activities in rural farming communities
options.B: To fund the construction of large international airports in every state capital
options.C: To make healthcare workers richer through direct salary commission bonuses
options.D: To discourage consumption and lower the population's risk of developing NCDs

explanation: Spot on! When unhealthy items become more expensive, people tend to buy less of them, which helps lower community rates of lifestyle diseases. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T1#GNS313_U3_T1_h7)
